source_text: Ideo non solum eloquendo, sed etiam repetendo inculcat dogmatis sui esse proprium traducem animarum putare, quod etiam per similitudinem generantium corporum approbare conatur. Sicut animae - inquit - gignuntur ab animabus, ita figmentum corporis a corporis natura digeritur et sicut caro de carne, ita anima de anima. Sed pergamus ad reliqua: Sicut ergo auctor animarum Deus est, ita corporum auctor per concupiscentiam diabolus est, ut in viscatorio diaboli per concupiscentiam mulieris, unde diabolus aucupatur non animas, sed corpora.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore not only by speaking but also by repeating he impresses that it is proper of his dogma to think a vine-layer of souls, which he also tries to prove through the similarity of generating bodies. As souls, he says, are generated from souls, so the figment of the body is digested from the nature of the body and as flesh from flesh, so soul from soul. But let us proceed to the remaining: As therefore God is the author of souls, so the author of bodies through desire is the devil, so that in the birdlime of the devil through the desire of a woman, from where the devil snares not souls but bodies.

lemmas.lexica: LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: He therefore stresses, not merely by saying it but by repeating it, that belief in souls’ transmission by descent is characteristic of his doctrine. He also tries to establish it through the analogy of bodies generating offspring: ‘Just as souls are generated from souls, so the body’s formation is drawn from bodily nature; and as flesh comes from flesh, so soul comes from soul.’ But let us proceed to the rest: ‘Just as God is the author of souls, so the devil, through desire, is the author of bodies. Thus, in the devil’s birdlime, through a woman’s desire, the devil snares not souls but bodies—’

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Continues Mani’s exposition of flesh from flesh and spirit from spirit, explicitly quoted in sections 172–173.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
